concept_html:
Open-ended survey answers ("What could we improve?") arrive as thousands of short texts. A sentence embedding model turns each text into a fixed-length vector, so that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors. With the sentence-transformers library:

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vectors = model.encode(answers, batch_size=64, normalize_embeddings=True)

all-MiniLM-L6-v2 returns 384 numbers per text. With normalize_embeddings=True every vector has length 1, so the cosine similarity of two texts is their dot product: 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated.

Rules that keep embeddings usable:

  • One model per analysis. Vectors from different models, or different versions of one model, live in different spaces. Never compare or mix them. Record the model name and version with the vectors.
  • Cache the vectors. Encoding is the slow step. Store vectors with the text ID, the model name and a hash of the text, and re-encode only new or changed answers.
  • Clean lightly. Strip whitespace and drop empty answers. Do not stem or remove stop words: the model was trained on natural text.
  • Check the language. Many small models are English-only. Use a multilingual model for multi-country surveys, and test it on your own answers.
  • Handle zero vectors. An empty string can produce a vector you should not compare. Filter before encoding, and guard any division by a vector's length.

Embeddings reflect the text the model was trained on, including its biases. Read samples of what the model calls "similar" before you trust any grouping built on it.

sentence-transformers needs PyTorch, which this app cannot run in the browser and this course's build could not install. The API details above are taken from the library's documentation and marked as not run here. The exercises use NumPy on vectors.

def top_k_similar(query: np.ndarray, matrix: np.ndarray, k: int) -> list[int]:
"""Row indices of the k rows most cosine-similar to query, most similar first."""
q_norm = np.linalg.norm(query)
raise ValueError("query vector has zero length")
norms = np.linalg.norm(matrix, axis=1)
sims = np.full(len(matrix), -np.inf)
sims[ok] = (matrix[ok] @ query) / (norms[ok] * q_norm)
return [int(i) for i in np.argsort(-sims, kind="stable")[:k]]

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np


def top_k_similar(query: np.ndarray, matrix: np.ndarray, k: int) -> list[int]:
    """Row indices of the k rows most cosine-similar to query.

    Args:
        query: Vector of length d.
        matrix: Array of shape (n, d).
        k: Number of indices to return.

    Returns:
        Indices, most similar first. Zero-length rows rank last.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If query has zero length.
    """
    q_norm = np.linalg.norm(query)
    if q_norm == 0:
        raise ValueError("query vector has zero length")
    norms = np.linalg.norm(matrix, axis=1)
    sims = np.full(len(matrix), -np.inf)
    ok = norms > 0
    sims[ok] = (matrix[ok] @ query) / (norms[ok] * q_norm)
    return [int(i) for i in np.argsort(-sims, kind="stable")[:k]]

title: Sentence embeddings for open-ended answers
why_html: An analyst embedded wave 1 answers with one model and, a year later, wave 2 answers with a newer model under the same short name. Similarity between the waves came out low across the board, and the report said themes had "shifted dramatically". The texts had not changed much. The two sets of vectors came from different spaces.
